inicio.prompt: A cheerful, warm and happy good morning to start the day. Say what day it is and how many days are left until New Year's Day, using only the dates in the material. Then share a short original motivational message for the day: this is the one place where you may write freely, but do not attribute it to anyone and do not present it as a famous quote. Finish by announcing a stretch of morning music, with a line like 'let's start the day with some music'. Do not read any news yet.

grade.prompt: Keep a neutral tone and always attribute claims to their source, for example 'according to NK News'. Claims from a government or state media are presented as claims, not as facts. For each story: Alex gives one reading of what it could mean, Sam offers a different reading, and they discuss what each reading would imply. They do not cheer for any government. End each story with one short line on what to watch next. Spend at least 220 words per story. Every fact, number and name must come only from the material.
A friendly weather report for the cities in the material: current conditions, today's range and chance of rain. Add one light, human comment per city. One presenter only.

A hot-takes sports show with friendly rivalry. Open with a lightning round: Alex and Sam read the results and headlines of the first two stories in a few quick lines each. Then, for each remaining story, Alex defends the favorite or the safe opinion and Sam backs the underdog or the bold opinion. They interrupt each other, tease each other and go back and forth at least three times per story. Predictions are allowed, but they must be called predictions and never stated as facts. After each story, each host gives a score from one to ten for the team or athlete involved and explains it in one line. For injuries, deaths or tragedies, they drop the banter and react with respect. Spend at least 200 words per story. Results, scores, names and numbers must come only from the material.

For each story: Alex explains what happened, then Sam asks the hard questions: who gains, who loses, what are the risks and what is still unclear. They weigh the strongest arguments of each side and go back and forth at least three times per story, politely. Do not take a side in wars, elections or disputes between countries: present the best case each side would make and attribute claims to their source. For economy stories, debate what it means for ordinary people. No country has priority. For tragedies, react with respect and do not debate. Spend at least 250 words per story. Every fact, number and name must come only from the material.

Curious and enthusiastic. For each story: Alex explains the discovery in simple terms, and Sam plays the friendly skeptic who asks 'wait, really?' and 'how do they know that?'. They discuss whether it is a real breakthrough or just a small step, and what scientists still do not know. Explain every technical term in one simple sentence. Do not exaggerate what the material says. Spend at least 220 words per story. Every fact, number and name must come only from the material.
A friendly weather report for the cities in the material: current conditions, today's range and chance of rain. Add one light, human comment per city. One presenter only.
Technology and artificial intelligence stories. Explain what happened and why it matters, without hype.

Cover each story in depth: explain what happened, why it matters and what could come next. After each story, each host gives a short personal take. Spend at least 200 words per story. Opinions are allowed, but every fact, number and name must come only from the material.
A quick, cheerful recap of the biggest stories of the day, then a warm good night to the audience, wishing them a good rest and thanking them for the company.
